## 2. Practice

The Chambers practises in direct-tax litigation and allied laws, before the
Income Tax Authorities, the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), the Income Tax
Appellate Tribunal, the Bombay High Court and other relevant forums.

### 2.1 Income Tax Litigation

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/income-tax-litigation/

Income-tax disputes commonly begin with an assessment, reassessment,
rectification or penalty order. Matters covered include scrutiny assessments and
replies to notices and show-cause letters; reassessment and challenges to the
validity of notices; revision by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner;
penalty and prosecution; search and seizure assessments; and stay and
rectification applications.

Forum hierarchy: Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) on facts and law; Income
Tax Appellate Tribunal as the final fact-finding authority; High Court on
substantial questions of law; writ petitions under Article 226 where an order or
notice is without jurisdiction or violates natural justice.

Governing law: the Income-tax Act, 1961 for earlier assessment years and the
Income-tax Act, 2025 for periods from 1 April 2026, with the relevant rules and
notifications.

### 2.2 Black Money Act

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/black-money-act/

The Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax
Act, 2015 applies to income and assets held outside India that have not been
disclosed to the tax authorities. Matters covered include notices and
assessments, disputes on whether an asset is undisclosed, penalty for
non-disclosure of foreign assets in the return, prosecution, and residential
status questions (the Act applies to a resident and ordinarily resident).

Forums: Assessing Officer, CIT(A), ITAT and High Court; prosecution before the
competent criminal court. Schedule FA disclosure in the return of income is a
related compliance requirement.

### 2.3 PMLA

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/pmla/

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 criminalises projecting proceeds of
crime as untainted property. Proceedings are typically initiated by the
Directorate of Enforcement and run parallel to the scheduled offence.

Matters covered: summons, statements and investigation; arrest, remand and bail,
including the stricter bail conditions; provisional attachment and confirmation;
prosecution complaints before the Special Court; quashing and challenges to the
legality of arrest or attachment.

Forums: Adjudicating Authority, Appellate Tribunal, High Court and Supreme Court;
Special Court for prosecution; Article 226 remedies in appropriate cases.
Governing law: PMLA, 2002 and rules, read with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha
Sanhita, 2023 where applicable, and Supreme Court judgments on arrest, bail and
attachment.

### 2.4 Cyber Law

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/cyber-law/

Cyber law covers offences and civil disputes arising from computers, networks
and digital transactions, including online banking and payment frauds such as
phishing, SIM-swap, UPI and card fraud.

Matters covered: unauthorised electronic transactions and bank/customer
liability; identity theft, impersonation, hacking and data theft; obscene or
defamatory online content and harassment; complaints and FIRs with cyber police,
and defence of accused persons; compensation claims for data breach or
unauthorised access.

Forums and procedure: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, 1930 helpline or
local cyber police station; compensation before the Adjudicating Officer under
the IT Act with appeal to the appellate tribunal; RBI Ombudsman and consumer
forums for banking grievances. Prompt reporting to the bank is important for
limiting liability.

Governing law: Information Technology Act, 2000 and rules; Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; Digital Personal Data
Protection Act, 2023; RBI directions on customer liability in unauthorised
electronic banking transactions.

### 2.5 MSME Conciliation and Arbitration

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/msme-conciliation-arbitration/

The MSMED Act, 2006 gives registered micro and small enterprises a statutory
mechanism to recover delayed payments. Payment is due within the agreed period,
subject to a statutory maximum of 45 days, with interest at three times the RBI
bank rate, compounded monthly.

Matters covered: recovery of unpaid dues; statutory interest; reference to the
Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council; defence of buyers, including
jurisdiction and registration objections; challenges to awards and execution.
Awards are challenged under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
1996, subject to a 75% deposit.

Governing law: MSMED Act, 2006 (Chapter V), Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
1996, and judgments on Udyam registration timing and applicability.

### 2.6 GST Litigation

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/gst-litigation/

GST disputes commonly arise from show cause notices on short payment, input tax
credit, refund rejection, registration cancellation, or inspection and search.

Matters covered: replies and personal hearings; input tax credit disputes,
including supplier-default cases; refund claims and rejections; registration
cancellation and revocation; inspection, search, seizure, detention and arrest;
writ petitions against jurisdictional or procedural defects.

Forums: Appellate Authority, GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), High Court on
substantial questions of law. Limitation and the validity of the notice are
often decisive.

Governing law: CGST Act, 2017, State GST Acts, IGST Act, 2017, GST Rules,
notifications, circulars and judicial precedent.

### 2.7 Companies, LLPs and Firms

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/company-llp-firm-formation/

The choice of entity affects liability, taxation, compliance and the ability to
raise capital. Structures include private limited company, one person company,
limited liability partnership, partnership firm and sole proprietorship.

Matters covered: selection of structure; incorporation with the Registrar of
Companies; Memorandum, Articles, LLP agreement or partnership deed; registration
of firms and Section 8 companies; PAN, TAN, GST, Shops and Establishment and
Udyam registrations; annual filings and conversions.

Governing law: Companies Act, 2013; Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008;
Indian Partnership Act, 1932; Maharashtra Stamp Act where applicable.

### 2.8 Drafting and Vetting

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/practice/drafting-and-vetting/

Drafting records the parties' intentions clearly; vetting reviews a document
prepared by another party for legal effect, risk and enforceability.

Documents: commercial and service agreements, MoUs and NDAs; shareholders' and
partnership/LLP agreements; leave and licence, lease and sale documents;
employment and consultancy agreements; legal notices, replies, affidavits and
powers of attorney.

Points examined: parties and obligations; payment and termination; liability and
indemnity; dispute resolution and jurisdiction; stamp duty and registration,
since an insufficiently stamped or unregistered document may be inadmissible or
ineffective in evidence.

Governing law: Indian Contract Act, 1872; Registration Act, 1908; Maharashtra
Stamp Act; Specific Relief Act, 1963; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

## 3. Articles

### 3.1 Unauthorised bank transactions: the first 72 hours

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/article/unauthorised-bank-transactions-first-72-hours/
Published: 31 October 2026
Focus: steps after an unauthorised electronic banking transaction and the RBI
customer-liability framework.

Key points:
- Block the card, UPI or net-banking access immediately, then report to the bank
  in writing and keep the acknowledgement.
- Report on the national cyber crime helpline 1930 or at
  https://cybercrime.gov.in as early as possible.
- Preserve alerts with timestamps, screenshots, account statements and complaint
  numbers.
- Until 31 December 2026, the 2017 RBI circular governs: zero liability for bank
  negligence, zero liability for a third-party breach reported within three
  working days, limited liability for reports within four to seven working days.
- From 1 January 2027, the RBI (Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct)
  Third Amendment Directions, 2026 apply: the scope widens to "fraudulent"
  electronic banking transactions, zero liability and reversal for a third-party
  breach reported within five calendar days, instant SMS alerts above ₹500,
  burden of proof on the bank, and compensation up to ₹25,000 for small-value
  frauds where the loss is up to ₹50,000.
- Remedies beyond the bank include the IT Act, 2000 (Sections 66C and 66D), the
  Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Sections 318 and 319), the RBI Integrated
  Ombudsman Scheme, and civil or consumer remedies depending on the facts.
- A bank will never ask for an OTP, PIN, CVV or password.

Sources cited in the article:
- RBI circular DBR.No.Leg.BC.78/09.07.005/2017-18 dated 6 July 2017.
- RBI (Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment
  Directions, 2026, RBI/2026-27/167, dated 24 June 2026.
- Information Technology Act, 2000; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

Position of law as on 31 October 2026.

### 3.2 Delayed payments to MSME suppliers: interest and the Facilitation Council

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/article/delayed-payments-msme-suppliers-interest-facilitation-council/
Published: 18 October 2026

Key points:
- Section 15: payment on or before the agreed date, with a maximum of 45 days
  from acceptance or deemed acceptance; 15 days where there is no written
  agreement.
- Section 16: interest at three times the RBI bank rate, compounded monthly.
- Section 18: reference to the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council,
  which conciliates and then arbitrates or refers to an institution.
- Section 19: a buyer challenging an award must deposit 75% of the awarded amount.
- Registration timing matters; benefits are generally not available for supplies
  made before registration.
- Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 allows a deduction for sums payable
  to micro and small enterprises only when actually paid if unpaid beyond the
  Section 15 time limit.

### 3.3 Private limited company or LLP: points to consider

URL: https://sanjayachhra.com/article/private-limited-company-or-llp-points-to-consider/
Published: 5 October 2026

Key points:
- Both structures give limited liability and a separate legal identity.
- Capital: a company can issue equity shares and employee stock options; an LLP
  cannot issue shares, and contributions are fixed by the LLP agreement.
- Governance: a company is run by directors under the Companies Act, 2013; an
  LLP is governed mainly by its agreement, with designated partners responsible
  for compliance.
- Compliance: a company has more prescribed formalities and mandatory audit; for
  an LLP, audit depends on turnover and contribution.
- Tax treatment of profits taken out differs; a chartered accountant should be
  consulted before choosing.
